extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors preparing for math olympiads / problem solvers in number theory (high-school and undergraduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, examples, and problems in elementary number theory aimed at solving Olympiad-style diophantine, divisibility, modular, and combinatorial number-theory problems. Emphasizes methods like factorization in quadratic fields, infinite descent, congruences, counting and pigeonhole arguments, and continued fractions for Pell equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization for Pell-type equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the identity x^2 − d y^2 = (x − y√d)(x + y√d) to study integer solutions of x^2 − d y^2 = 1 (and related equations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this factorization one deduces multiplicative closure: the product or quotient of two solutions is again a solution. For positive solutions, note x + y√d > 1 and x − y√d < 1; these inequalities are used in ordering arguments and to generate new solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate all Pell solutions from the fundamental unit
rubrics_metrics.description: If x0 + y0√d is the smallest positive solution of x^2 − d y^2 = 1, then every solution is (x0 + y0√d)^n for some integer n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by the method of descent: assume another solution lies between consecutive powers of x0 + y0√d, multiply by an appropriate power of (x0 − y0√d) and reach a contradiction with minimality. Thus it suffices to find the minimal positive solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find minimal Pell solution via continued fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: The minimal positive solution (x0, y0) of x^2 − d y^2 = 1 can be found by developing √d into a continued fraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If x0 and y0 are small, exhaustive search at contests may suffice; for general d, use the periodic continued-fraction expansion of √d to compute the fundamental solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use congruences to rule out solvability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use congruence (modular arithmetic) arguments to show certain diophantine equations have no solutions (for example, x^2 − d y^2 = −1 often has no solutions detectable by congruences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check residues modulo small moduli to obtain contradictions (e.g., squares modulo 3,7,8,9 used repeatedly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of infinite descent for impossibility/minimality proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply infinite descent to show nonexistence of nontrivial solutions or to force minimality to a contradiction (used for Pell minimality arguments and many diophantine impossibility proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical pattern: assume a minimal counterexample exists, then construct a strictly smaller counterexample, contradiction. Used e.g. in sums-of-squares and many x^2 + ... type problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use irrationality + inequalities to prove sequence properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For exponential sequences f(n)=α^n and g(n)=β^n with irrational α,β and 1/α + 1/β = 1, prove sequences are disjoint and their union is N by bounding arguments exploiting irrationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume equality α^m = β^n = q + fractional_part and derive inequalities q < α^m < q+1 and q < β^n < q+1; combine to get impossible inequalities for reciprocals, using irrationality to avoid exact integer coincidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding inequalities to characterize images/missed values of sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a function like f(n)=n + √(n + 1/2) or f(n)=n + √(2n + 1/2), compare f(n) with integers m and m+1 to deduce algebraic inequalities constraining m−n, which classify which integers the sequence attains or omits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform the inequalities to quadratic bounds in (m−n) and use simple counting or parity to identify omitted values (e.g., shows sequence misses exactly the squares or triangular numbers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting / pigeonhole arguments for representation counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Count numbers in intervals or classes (e.g., number of squares ≤ k^2 + k is k, number of values of a sequence up to N) to deduce surjectivity/omission and other mapping properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine elementary counting with previously derived inequalities to conclude exact counts of values attained or omitted by sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity and small-modulus residue classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parity and residues modulo small integers (mod 2,3,4,8,9,11, etc.) to rule out possibilities or force structure of solutions (e.g., classify which n are sums of three squares; odd square ≡1 mod 8; squares modulo 3 or 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out all possible residues of squares modulo the modulus, then check combinations to deduce impossibilities or necessary congruences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic divisibility and Fermat-type tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply standard divisibility facts (e.g., a^p ≡ a (mod p), Fermat's little theorem) and factorization identities (an − bn divisible by a − b, etc.) to establish divisibility properties used in contest problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as quick tests for primality divisibility patterns and to factor expressions into products of consecutive integers when applicable (e.g., n^5 − n has small prime divisors because of factorization into consecutive factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean algorithm and gcd-based manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute gcd relations and use properties gcd(a,b)=gcd(a,b−ka) to deduce divisibility results, reduce diophantine equations, and simplify congruences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reduce gcd(2n+3,n+7) to gcd(n−4,11); deduce when gcd equals 1 or 11 depending on n mod 11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization identities to restrict solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform diophantine expressions into factorized forms (e.g., (x^2−1)(y^2−1)=1) to force limited integer possibilities and conclude triviality or finiteness of solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite equations to exhibit small factors or direct multiplicative constraints, then analyze factor pairs to get integer solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digit/base representation methods for decimal puzzles
rubrics_metrics.description: Model digit problems (moving digits, palindromes under multiplication, automorphic numbers) by writing numbers as 10^k·prefix + rest and setting up congruences or linear equations in digits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve resulting congruences modulo powers of 10 and use divisibility by small numbers (e.g., 9, 11, 17) to narrow digit choices; use modular constraints to find unique solutions (examples: 2178, 7125, automorphic numbers 5,6,25,76,376,9376, ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting prime-power exponents in factorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the exponent of a prime p in n! using floor-sum n/p + n/p^2 + n/p^3 + ..., to answer questions like how many trailing zeros or multiplicity of prime factors occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to compute trailing zeros (number of 5s), or to compare exponents for divisibility of binomial-type products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariance and sign-change counting in combinatorial sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use invariants (products, parity, sign-change counts) to deduce structural results in problems involving ±1 sequences around a circle or similar setups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., relate number of sign changes to product patterns; count how often pairs produce −1; use multiplicative invariants to force divisibility or parity constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy & threshold analysis for combinatorial games (Euclid-type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze take-away games by comparing pile sizes and finding threshold ratios (e.g., if a > 2b first player can force win), then generalize to find the critical α for which first player has a forced win.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use size comparisons, greedy reductions, and invariants of moves (taking multiples of other pile) to devise winning strategies; relate to continued-fraction like reductions of Euclid's algorithm.
